It’s just been going on long enough that it’s affecting how I think about the work, and I figured I should talk to someone.\n\nDoctor: Do you think it’s possible you might be mistaken about your coworkers coordinating against you?\n\nPatient: I mean… I’ve tried to ask myself that, honestly. But no, I don’t really think I’m mistaken. Not in the overall thing.\n\nLike, sure, any one piece by itself could be nothing — a seating change, someone making a comment in rehearsal, a schedule adjustment. I know that. In grad school we used to joke about how conductors read meaning into everything, like if the violas look tired suddenly it’s a political statement or something… sorry, that’s not really the point.\n\nThe point is that after that commission, it became a pattern. A few people in the ensemble kept doing these little things that, put together, felt very clearly meant to undermine me. And when I bring it up, they show me emails or notes like that explains it, but to me it just doesn’t account for the way it keeps lining up. So… possible in theory, I guess, but I can’t shake the certainty that something coordinated is happening.\n\nDoctor: Have you ever been absolutely certain of something like this and later found out it wasn’t true?\n\nPatient: Not really. I mean, I’ve been wrong about small things before, obviously — like rehearsal logistics, who sent what email, that kind of boring administrative stuff. There was one time in school I was convinced a score marking meant one thing and it was just, you know, a copyist’s habit, but that’s not the same.\n\nWith this… no. I haven’t had a moment where I found out the whole thing wasn’t true. It’s more that for almost two years I haven’t been able to shake it — that after that commission, a few people started using these little schedule changes, seating choices, comments in rehearsal, all of it, to quietly undermine the work. And they’ll show me emails or notes like that explains it, but it never really explains why it keeps lining up the way it does.\n\nDoctor: Have you ever felt that someone was controlling your thoughts or putting thoughts into your mind?\n\nPatient: No, I don’t think so. I mean… “controlling my thoughts” sounds like something more direct than what I’m talking about.\n\nSometimes a phrase someone says at rehearsal gets stuck in my head, but that happens with music too — like a bad interval or one line of text repeating for hours, which is annoying but not exactly someone putting it there. So… no, I haven’t felt like my thoughts were being controlled.\n\nDoctor: Have you been hearing voices when no one is there?\n\nPatient: No… not like voices when nobody’s there. I mean, I’m around sound constantly, so sometimes I’ll think I hear a note or a fragment of something after rehearsal, like my brain keeps replaying it. That happens a lot with music, actually — you know, if the oboe comes in sharp in the same place three times, it sort of haunts you later.\n\nBut actual voices, like someone speaking to me when no one is there? I don’t think so.\n\nDoctor: Before all this started at work, did you generally tend to distrust other people’s motives?\n\nPatient: I’m not sure, honestly. I don’t think I went around assuming everyone had bad motives, if that’s what you mean. I mean, in music there’s always a certain amount of reading people — conductors, players, committees — because someone can say, “That’s interesting,” and it means six different things depending on the room.\n\nBut that feels more like… professional caution, maybe? Like learning not to take every compliment at face value. I don’t remember thinking most people were against me before this. I’d have to think about it.\n\nDoctor: Aside from dealing with this situation at work, have you become less able to manage your usual work or daily life than you used to?\n\nPatient: Not really, no. I mean, work is… complicated because of the ensemble situation, obviously. But outside of that, I’m still functioning. I still meet deadlines, I’m keeping up with composing, and I run most mornings — actually, running is where I get a lot of my best rhythmic ideas, which sounds pretentious, but it’s true.\n\nAnd at home, things with my wife are basically steady. I wouldn’t say I’ve fallen apart or stopped managing day-to-day life. It’s more that this one situation takes up too much space in my head.\n\nDoctor: Outside of this situation at work, do you also feel that other people are deliberately trying to harm, watch, or undermine you?\n\nPatient: Not really outside of the ensemble, no. It’s mostly centered there. I mean, I’m here because I can’t get past this feeling — certainty, really — that after that commission, a few people in the group started doing these little things to undercut me. Schedule changes, who gets seated where, comments in rehearsal that sound harmless if you write them down, but in the room they’re not harmless.\n\nAnd then they’ll show me an email or some note, like, “See, this was just logistical,” but it doesn’t settle it for me. It still feels coordinated. But no, I’m not walking around thinking strangers or neighbors are watching me or anything like that. It’s tied to work.\n\nDoctor: Did this belief about your coworkers start suddenly, over a few days, rather than building up gradually?\n\nPatient: I don’t know if I’d call it sudden. It’s hard to pin down, because at the time you’re not thinking, “Oh, here’s the start of something.” You’re just in rehearsal, or checking messages, or noticing the way someone phrases something.\n\nI guess it felt like it accumulated, but then there were moments where it sort of snapped into focus. Like in music, you can hear a motif a few times before you realize it’s the thing organizing the whole piece. Sorry, that’s probably not the most direct answer. I’m not sure it was over just a few days.\n\nDoctor: Since this started, have you had a period when you felt unusually high, energized, or needed much less sleep?\n\nPatient: I’m not sure. I mean, there are times I get absorbed in work and stay up late because I’m writing or revising something, but that’s sort of always been part of how I work. Composers have terrible boundaries with sleep—well, maybe that’s just me and everyone I went to school with.\n\nBut unusually high or energized… I don’t know. I wouldn’t describe it that way. I’ve been tense, maybe preoccupied, but not like suddenly I’m invincible or anything. And the sleep thing is hard because rehearsals, deadlines, coffee… it all blurs together. I haven’t really noticed a clear period like that.\n\nDoctor: Before this started at work, did you often suspect that other people were trying to deceive or take advantage of you?\n\nPatient: I’m not sure I’d put it that way. I mean, I’ve always been… maybe cautious? In music school you learn pretty quickly that people can be competitive, and there’s always this weird thing where someone says they loved your piece and then you hear later they were criticizing it in the hallway. But that’s also just artists being artists, I guess.\n\nBefore all this at work, I don’t think I was walking around assuming people were trying to take advantage of me, no. I could get irritated or wonder what someone meant by something, but it wasn’t like this constant suspicion. I don’t think so, anyway.\n\nDoctor: Before this work situation began, did you often hold grudges for a long time after feeling insulted or slighted?\n\nPatient: I don’t know. I mean, I remember things people say—probably more than I should—but I don’t think I was sitting around keeping a ledger of insults or anything.\n\nIt’s funny, in ensembles people can be so casually cutting, like one comment about your tempo choice and suddenly you’re thinking about it while brushing your teeth two days later. But that’s maybe just being sensitive, or caring too much about the work. I wouldn’t say I often held grudges for a long time before this, not in some major way. I might replay things, but then usually something else would come up and I’d move on.\n\nDoctor: Have you become less emotionally expressive or less interested in other people than you used to be?\n\nPatient: Less expressive? I don’t know. Maybe I’ve been more tired in conversations, but I wouldn’t say I’ve become… flat or anything.\n\nInterested in other people—again, that’s hard, because when I’m working on a score I can forget to answer texts for two days, and then suddenly I’m at a rehearsal having to care very intensely about what a clarinetist thinks of one entrance. But then when it keeps lining up in these little ways after the commission, it’s hard to just… swallow the official version.\n\nSo I don’t know if “clear proof” would feel clear to me. I’d probably still wonder what wasn’t being shown. Which sounds bad when I say it out loud, but that’s where I am.\n\nDoctor: Has there been even one time when you fully accepted that a specific incident you thought was part of the coordination was actually innocent?\n\nPatient: Fully accepted?
